lines: Fold a sheet of paper in half, forty-two times. How thick is it now?
A. As tall as a house. B. As high as Mount Everest. C. It reaches the Moon.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A says: it's paper. Fold it as much as you like, it's still just paper.
Team B goes bigger. Maybe a mountain?
And Team C sounds ridiculous. A tenth of a millimetre... to the Moon?
But every fold doubles the thickness.
Ten folds: over a thousand layers. About ten centimetres.
Twenty folds: about a hundred metres. Taller than Big Ben.
Thirty folds: over a hundred kilometres. That's past the edge of space.
And forty-two folds: about four hundred and forty thousand kilometres.
The Moon is only about three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres away.
So it's C. That's exponential growth: doubling, again and again. And yes, it's on your GCSE maths spec.
The catch? You can't actually do it.
In 2002, a student called Britney Gallivan set the record: twelve folds. She needed a roll of paper over a kilometre long.
More maths that sounds fake but isn't? Follow Full Marks.
A tree grows from a tiny seed. Where does all that wood come from?
A. Thin air. B. The soil. C. The water it drinks.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A sounds ridiculous. Air weighs almost nothing.
Team B says the soil. That's where the roots are.
Team C says water. Trees soak up loads of it.
Nearly four hundred years ago, Jan van Helmont tested it.
He planted a willow in dried, weighed soil, and gave it only water.
Five years later, the tree had gained about seventy-four kilograms.
The soil had lost about fifty-seven grams. The mass of an egg.
So it's not the soil. The secret ingredient is in the air: carbon dioxide.
In photosynthesis, leaves use light to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose.
The tree links glucose into cellulose, the main material in wood.
Dry wood is nearly half carbon, and all of that carbon came from the air.
So it's A. Most of a tree's dry mass is made from air. It's on your GCSE biology spec.
The catch? Van Helmont misread his own experiment. He thought it was all water.
Biology that sounds fake but isn't? Follow Full Marks.
Which is bigger: glasses of water in all the oceans, or molecules in one glass?
A. The oceans, easily. B. One glass. C. About the same.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A says: it's every ocean on Earth!
Team B says molecules are tiny, so there must be loads.
Team C says both are huge. Call it a draw.
One glass: about two hundred and fifty millilitres, so two hundred and fifty grams of water.
The oceans hold about one point three billion cubic kilometres: about five times ten to the twenty-one glasses.
Water's relative formula mass is eighteen. So our glass is about fourteen moles.
One mole is six point oh two times ten to the twenty-three molecules: the Avogadro constant.
So one glass holds about eight times ten to the twenty-four molecules.
That's about fifteen hundred times more than all those glasses.
So it's B. And it's on your GCSE chemistry spec: moles, higher tier.
The catch? Tag every molecule, tip the glass into the sea, and mix it perfectly through every ocean.
Scoop out a glass, and you'd find about fifteen hundred of your tagged molecules.
Chemistry with numbers this big? Follow Full Marks.
Astronauts float on the Space Station. So how strong is gravity up there?
A. Zero. B. About half. C. About ninety percent.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A says: they're floating. Case closed.
Team B says: they're way above the Earth, so gravity must be much weaker.
Team C points at the Moon. It's way further out, and Earth's gravity still holds it.
Here's the maths: g equals G M over r squared, and r is measured from Earth's centre.
Earth's radius is about six thousand four hundred kilometres. Add four hundred for the station: six thousand eight hundred.
Square that ratio, and g only drops from nine point eight to about eight point seven newtons per kilogram.
So why do they float? They're in free fall, along with the whole station.
It moves sideways at nearly eight kilometres per second, so it keeps falling around the Earth, and missing.
So it's C: about ninety percent. Gravitational fields are on your A-level physics spec.
The catch? On top of a tower four hundred kilometres tall, you'd still feel nearly ninety percent of your normal weight.
Floating isn't about height. It's about falling. Follow Full Marks.
Volunteers are told to shock a stranger, up to four hundred and fifty volts. How many go all the way?
A. About two thirds. B. About a third. C. Hardly anyone.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A says people do what they're told.
Team B says most would stop once the other person protested.
Team C has backup: Yale psychology students predicted about one in a hundred.
Milgram's obedience study: Yale, early nineteen sixties, forty men.
Each man was the teacher, giving a bigger shock for every wrong answer.
The switches went up in fifteen-volt steps.
At three hundred volts, the learner pounded on the wall. Soon after, he went silent.
If a teacher hesitated, he was prodded: 'Please continue.' 'The experiment requires that you continue.'
Every teacher went to at least three hundred volts.
Twenty-six out of forty went all the way: sixty-five percent.
So it's A. Milgram's obedience research is on your A-level psychology spec.
The catch? The learner was in on it. Nobody was really shocked.
But the teachers believed it. Many sweated, trembled and stuttered, and most kept going.
Psychology that changes how you see people? Follow Full Marks.
Melting ice takes in heat. So why does it happen all by itself?
A. The warm room forces it. B. It's secretly exothermic. C. Disorder goes up: entropy.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A says the warm room pours heat in.
Team B says it must release hidden energy.
Team C says it's about disorder, not just heat.
Year thirteen A-level chemistry: entropy, S. Ice is ordered; liquid water, more disordered.
Melting raises entropy by twenty-two joules per kelvin per mole.
Gibbs free energy: delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. Feasible when delta G is zero or negative.
Melting takes in six point oh one kilojoules per mole. Set delta G to zero, solve for T.
Six thousand and ten over twenty-two: two hundred and seventy-three kelvin. Zero degrees Celsius.
Above that, T delta S beats delta H, delta G goes negative, and ice melts.
Team A gets half a point: temperature multiplies the entropy term.
So it's C. Entropy and Gibbs free energy are on your A-level chemistry spec.
The catch? Freezing gives out heat, yet above zero degrees, water never freezes.
Exothermic isn't enough. Disorder gets a vote. Follow Full Marks.
Blood leaves your lungs full of oxygen. At rest, how much do your cells actually take out?
A. Nearly all of it. B. About a quarter. C. About half.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A says cells are greedy. Why send any back?
Team B says your body keeps a reserve.
Team C says split it: half out, half back.
Year twelve A-level biology: the oxygen dissociation curve.
In the lungs, oxygen partial pressure is high, so haemoglobin loads to about ninety-eight percent saturation.
In resting tissues, it only falls to about five kilopascals.
There, haemoglobin is still about three quarters saturated. So on average, your body takes about a quarter.
But that's the steep part of the S-shaped curve. A small drop in partial pressure releases much more oxygen.
Busy muscles make more carbon dioxide. Haemoglobin's affinity drops, the curve shifts right: the Bohr effect.
So it's B. Haemoglobin and the Bohr effect are on your A-level biology spec.
The catch? That's an average. Your heart muscle takes well over half, even at rest.
So a harder-working heart can't take much more. It needs more blood flow.
Biology with a built-in reserve? Follow Full Marks.
All eight billion people on Earth, in one alphabetical list. At most, how many checks to find one name?
A. About eight billion. B. Thirty-three. C. About ninety thousand.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A checks names one by one: up to eight billion.
Team B says halve the list every time.
Team C picks the square root. Ninety thousand sounds clever.
This is binary search, from A-level computer science.
Check the middle name. Is your target before it or after it?
Either way, one check throws away half the list.
Eight billion becomes four billion, then two billion, then one billion, and so on.
Two to the power thirty-three is about eight point six billion. So thirty-three halvings cover everyone.
A linear search could need eight billion checks. That's big O of n, against big O of log n.
So it's B: thirty-three checks, at most. Time complexity is on your A-level computer science spec.
The catch? It only works if the list is already sorted. Sorting eight billion names is the slow part.
Double the world to sixteen billion, and you need just one more check. Follow Full Marks.
Perfect weather. Farmers grow their biggest harvest ever. What happens to their total revenue?
A. It falls. B. It rises. C. It stays the same.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A smells a trick question.
Team B says more to sell means more money.
Team C says prices drop, so it all evens out.
This is Year twelve A-level economics: price elasticity of demand.
A bumper harvest shifts supply to the right, so the price falls.
Food is a necessity. Cheaper bread doesn't make us eat much more: demand is price inelastic.
Say farmers usually sell a hundred units at three pounds: three hundred pounds.
The bumper crop is a hundred and ten units. To sell them, the price falls to two pounds.
Revenue: two hundred and twenty pounds. Ten percent more crop, over a quarter less revenue.
With inelastic demand, price and total revenue move in the same direction.
So it's A. Elasticity and total revenue are on your A-level economics spec.
The catch? For one farmer alone, a bumper crop is great. The price barely moves.
It only hurts when every farmer has one: the fallacy of composition.
Economics that sounds backwards? Follow Full Marks.
